Q: Why does sorting reduce the time of my function? A:

Why sort speeds up readarray : A case of I/O Serialization complexity and system overhead

While sort adds O(n log n) operations, it solves a massive bottleneck in how Bash manages memory and process synchronization.

The Slow Path :

 When  you run
 (seq 0 20000) readarray -t array ; 
 two processes are fighting for resources.

  1. The Producer(seq): Floods the pipe buffer immediately.

  2. The Consumer(readarray): Must wake up, read a line, allocate memory(via malloc) and store it.

Because Bash is an interpreted shell it memory management is relatively slow. In this scenario, the kernel is constantly context switching between the producer and the consumer. Every time seq fills a bit of the pipe, readarray tries to empty it. The Handshaking creates massive overhead that far outweighs the actual data processing.

The Faster Path :

 When  you run
 (seq 0 20000|sort) readarray -t array;
 two processes are fighting for resources.

Adding sort changes the architecture from streaming to batching.

  1. The Dam Effect: sort is a "blocking" utility. It cannot output anything until it has read the very last line (EOF) because it doesn't know which line come first until the end.

  2. Serialization : While sort is running, readarray is blocked and idle. This eliminates context switching during the "Collection" phase. sort (Written in Highly optimized C) handles 20000 lines in its own internal memory space much faster than Bash can.

  3. Efficient Ingestion: Once sort finishes, it flushes its entire result set into the pipe at once. readarray then reads this data in large, contiguous bursts. The kernel can pass the data through the pipe much more efficiently because the "producer" (sort) is now just dumping a finished buffer rather than generating lines one by one.

Q: Pandoc Converting MD To HTML: WCAG-Uncompliant Links In Code Blocks A:

I think the comment "this is an issue with the accessibility checker ..." was correct. But I am mandated to try to satisfy the checker. I hesitate to call this a solution, but my work-around is to run pandoc's output through this:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
MoveEmptyAnchors.py

Removes from an HTML document all anchor elements that contain no content.

I am doing this because the YuJa Panorama LMS Accessibility Platform (and perhaps other compliance checkers) flag any such anchors as violations of Success Criterion 2.4.4, even if they have attributes telling screen readers to ignore them.

Links of this type are created by pandoc for each line in a syntax-highlighted code block, and removing them through pandoc is impossible because they do not appear in the AST.  I have written this script to post-process pandoc's output.

Author: Chad Hogg <chad.hogg@millersville.edu>
Created: 2026-01-31
"""

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import sys

soup = BeautifulSoup(sys.stdin.read(), 'html.parser')

for link in soup.find_all('a'):
    if not link.contents:
        link.decompose()

sys.stdout.write(str(soup))

Q: Is there a way to use the old remnants of Windows XP and 7's UI in Windows 11 with Python? A:

You would probably need to get copies of the Windows libraries from those systems in order to replicate the old look and feel. Whether they would work with Python is impossible to guess. As far as I am aware the only Windows interface library available with Python is pywin32. But that most likely just calls the SDK that is installed on your system.

Q: Get-AzAccessToken is failing with error "SharedTokenCacheCredential authentication unavailable" A:

This is a bit tricky, and I'm pretty sure none of the previous answers addressed the root cause. For me, I had to ensure that the app registration for which I was generating the token via az cli - Get-AzAccessToken -ResourceUrl "api://$CLIENT_ID" - included in the list of authorized apps - under "Expose an API" - included the first-party app "Microsoft Azure PowerShell" by id - specifically 1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2. See this link to get a list of all such first party apps.
